Seeing as how many languages exist today, I always thought about whether or not humans will eventually obtain a universal language. The world is big, but, with the advancement in communication recently, especially the Internet, shouldn't there be a chance that these technologies will continually connect us until we have universals, like languages?
Q: Will there ever be a universal language?

The issue isn't technology. It's people. We constantly change language. Get rid of people, replace us with machines that communicate, and it's possible.

Hundreds of years ago, a good hussy meant a good housewife. Don't call a woman a 'good hussy' today and expect a positive reaction. we change words for people.

200 years ago, coke was a fuel used in ironworking. We add meanings to existing words. (Runs in baseball do not equal runs in fabric do not equal having the runs).

Today, people play roleplaying games with blacksmiths in them, but blacksmiths today called themselves farriers, which is a historical name. We change words to make them more understandable.

Shell shock was an earlier name for combat fatigue. We change words to make them less scary or to manipulate people (depending on your point of view).

Cartwrights, wainwrights, fletchers, and boatswains were all careers. We change words as jobs change.

All of see the same things. Pictures are universal:

(https://www.ted.com/talks/ajit_narayanan_a_word_game_to_communicate_in_any_language)

There is already a universal language when it comes to programming and it is English.

As for the rest of the world using a universal language - while it is possible, there are many things preventing that from happening: Germany does a great deal of effort to dub (record over original actor voices with a German voice) all shows that air in movie theaters or TV throughout Germany. Same goes for China.

The same thing can be observed in France: while I was there, it was almost impossible to hear anyone speak English. All TV channels were in French with same dubbing technique that is in use in Germany.

On the other hand, you have countries like Sweden where no dubbing takes place and almost everyone is able to hold a conversation in English, regardless of their age. However, Swedish is the official language, used in universities and national TV, spoken on the streets, required to get a job... So, Swedish language is not threatened by all the English media.

Will there be a universal language in the end? I guess nobody knows but I sure hope so. Languages, while beautiful, affect the speed at which mankind in making technological advancements.

If we're talking about universal languages, there have been many, many deliberate attempts at creating such a language. Esperanto being one them and is perhaps the only truly successful attempt at creating an international auxiliary language.

While it was never intended to replace one's native language, Zamenhof's goal was "to create an easy-to-learn, politically neutral language that would transcend nationality and foster peace and international understanding between people with different languages."

Something that as an "armchair linguist" is a bit a of a sucker for.

While the language is barely 200 years old, the language itself is thriving and has been evidenced that learning it may provide a superior foundation for learning a foreign language.

Just my 2c..

Or who knows, maybe we'll find the Babel fish at the bottom of the ocean.

People who I don't agree with, have changed my mind on several different issues. I consider myself to be a reasonable man, and so even though I do have strong beliefs, if someone can convince me that my thinking is in error or incomplete, I will change it.

I try not to hold on the beliefs that I cannot rationalize to someone else. So the biggest thing I have gained from "losing", is that I have expanded my own mind, and gained better insight into how things really are. I rather admit loss and learn, rather than "win" and be wrong.

Other times I have learned that many of these "controversial" matters tend to lie in the grey area, rather than black and white as I might have wrongfully assumed.

My experiences have taught me to be open-minded enough to listen to other people's opinions, and to not hold on to ideas that I understand to be false, just for the sake of stubbornness and pride. It has also taught me why I shouldn't hate the people I disagree with, because some people unfortunately don't get the proper tools with which to critical think for themselves, and I should help them and work with them, than against them... because otherwise, no progress will ever be made.
